articles.title: A large trial of genotype-guided antidepressant prescribing finds no early benefit but higher remission later
articles.summary: Using genetic test results to guide antidepressant prescriptions did not improve depression symptoms after 3 months in a large clinical trial. But by 6 months, more patients in the gene-guided group had reached remission.

articles.title: The stronger the evidence, the weaker the link between prenatal acetaminophen and autism or ADHD
articles.summary: In September 2025, President Donald Trump advised pregnant women against taking acetaminophen, citing autism risk. A new review suggests the evidence behind that concern is weak, with apparent risks shrinking once lower-quality studies are set aside.

articles.title: Ketamine and psychedelics share a surprising link to the immune system
articles.summary: Ketamine and psychedelics relieve severe depression in hours, but their exact mechanisms remain elusive. New research suggests these rapid-acting drugs share a biological pathway, fighting depression by rebalancing specific immune system signals in the brain and body.

articles.title: People who ghost tend to feel worse about it than the people they ghost realize
articles.summary: Being ghosted can feel like proof the other person doesn’t care. But in studies of recalled and imagined conversations, people who stopped replying felt worse about it than those left waiting predicted, especially when the silence was accidental.

articles.title: The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast
articles.summary: Your daily routine could have a bigger impact on your ability to handle stress than you realize. A Binghamton University study of approximately 400 college students found that eating breakfast regularly, exercising, sleeping well, and taking fish oil were associated with greater psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to stressful situations. Poor sleep and unhealthy eating habits, meanwhile, were linked to lower flexibility and resilience.

articles.title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white matter, once thought to be relatively uniform, contains a complex patchwork of chemically distinct regions.

articles.title: This tiny jurassic predator helped pave the way for the human brain
articles.summary: A 165-million-year-old fossil has revealed an extraordinary Jurassic predator that may help explain how mammals developed one of their most important evolutionary advantages. Although only 20 inches long, Megacauda sungei was a heavyweight among early mammal relatives, swimming through ancient waterways and hunting prey with specialized teeth. Its advanced swallowing anatomy reveals an early step toward the ability to safely nurse on milk, a key development in mammalian evolution.

articles.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
articles.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.

articles.title: Musicians are less prone to the ventriloquism illusion, study finds
articles.summary: A flash of light can make a sound seem to come from the wrong place. Musicians are less susceptible to this illusion, a new study suggests, possibly because they are less inclined to assume the two share a source.

articles.summary: People who scored higher on a creative drawing test tended to have stronger white matter in pathways tied to movement and vision, according to a brain imaging study of 142 young adults in Austria.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Scientists uncover a possible trade-off in how the hippocampus replays new memories
articles.summary: When the brain rests after learning, it actively replays recent experiences. A new brain imaging study reveals this mental replay prioritizes general themes while stripping away specific details, suggesting false memories are a natural byproduct of learning.

articles.title: Is fatness a feminist issue?
articles.summary: Feminist scholars have long argued that anti-fat stigma is rooted in sexism. But when researchers asked fat women directly, many disagreed, some framing their weight as a personal matter, and a few even said fat women deserve to be teased.

articles.summary: Spiritual doubts are linked to higher anxiety in college students, but a new study finds that cultivating patience for everyday annoyances—like traffic and long lines—can independently predict a reduction in generalized anxiety over time.

articles.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.
